title: Ask the Tall Spears About Our High Deeds
intro: Safi al-Din al-Hilli wrote this as a young man, in pride at his tribe, the Sinbis of Tayyi', who in 701 AH (1301 CE) took revenge by force for his maternal uncle Safi al-Din, murdered in his own mosque by men of the house of Abu al-Fadl; so the heading in his diwan says. His editor Muhammad Mazloum adds that the poet fought in the battle of al-Zawra', was wounded there, and wrote the poem at twenty-three. It asks the spears and swords what happened, describes the horses and the young men, and mocks the enemy as starlings who took themselves for falcons and chess pawns who would have hunted queens; then come a broader boast of the tribe, praise of a sovereign power that protects it, and an enemy who hides treachery inside friendly advice. Ibn Fadl Allah al-Umari, the poet's contemporary, chose nineteen of its lines for his survey Masalik al-Absar, and Ali al-Tantawi recalls in his memoirs learning it by heart at school in Damascus.

1.1.3.meaning: Awali: the upper parts of spear shafts, below the head; also the spears themselves.

1.2.2.head: البيض
1.2.2.meaning: Bid: “the white ones”, swords, from the gleam of their blades.

2.2.3-5.meaning: Qabr Ubayd Allah, “Ubayd Allah's tomb”: a place in Iraq named after a shrine; the diwan's editors do not say which. Two shrines of the name were known in Iraq, the Mashhad al-Nudhur in Baghdad and the tomb of Ubayd Allah ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib at al-Madhar.

4.1.4-5.meaning: Zawra' of Iraq: Baghdad, once called al-Zawra'; other places bore the name too.

5.1.1.head: ضُمَّر
5.1.1.meaning: Dummar: lean horses, trained down for racing and war.

5.1.4.head: مُسَوَّمَة
5.1.4.meaning: Marked with a sign for battle; some say, put out to graze.

7.1.3.head: اِستَخصَمَ
7.1.3.meaning: Were challenged to a quarrel or a fight.

7.1.5.head: فَراعِنَة
7.1.5.meaning: Fara'ina: “pharaohs”, tyrants who bow to no one.

8.2.2.meaning: Wagha: war, from the din of battle.

10.1.4-5.meaning: “Their riser rose”: their cause rose up, they grew strong.

10.2.4.head: شَواهين
10.2.4.meaning: Shawahin: falcons, long-winged birds of prey.

11.1.3.head: البُزاة
11.1.3.meaning: Buzat: hawks, birds trained for the hunt.

12.1.1.head: بَيادِق
12.1.1.meaning: Bayadiq: pawns, the foot soldiers of chess.

12.2.4.head: فَرازين
12.2.4.meaning: Farazin: the chess vizier, the piece that later became the queen.

14.2.5.head: تَقاضي
14.2.5.meaning: Our demanding payment of a debt: here, revenge.

15.2.4.head: الدَّواوين
15.2.4.meaning: Dawawin: government offices, where officials and scribes sat.

17.2.3.head: عَبير
17.2.3.meaning: Abir: a perfume blended with saffron.

18.2.6.head: تَلقين
18.2.6.meaning: Talqin: dictating a lesson for a pupil to repeat and learn.

20.1.2.head: صَنائِع
20.1.2.meaning: Sana'i': favours, kindnesses done to others.

22.1.3.head: فَرامين
22.1.3.meaning: Faramin: firmans, a ruler's written decrees to his governors (from Persian).

23.1.6.head: طَلَق
23.1.6.meaning: Talaq: one heat of a horse race.

23.2.6.head: مُصَلّين
23.2.6.meaning: Musallin: horses that come second, with their heads at the winner's rump (sala).

24.2.3-4.meaning: “The turning of time”: its blows and reversals.

26.1.1.head: مُلك
26.1.1.meaning: Mulk: sovereignty, royal power; here the ruling power that protects them.

26.1.3.head: فَوَّقَ
26.1.3.meaning: Were notched: the arrow's nock set on the bowstring, ready to shoot.

27.1.4.head: ثاقِبَة
27.1.4.meaning: Piercing, blazing as if boring through the dark. The editions have it in the nominative, describing the resolves; the reciter says it in the accusative, describing them as they strike.

28.2.6.head: مَمنون
28.2.6.meaning: Cut off, or spoiled by reminding the receiver of the gift.

translation: Ask the tall spears about our high deeds,
and call the swords to witness: did hope in us ever fail?
1.sharh: He tells a woman to ask the weapons that were there: the spears and swords can testify to his people's glory and to hopes in them that were never let down. In Arabic “spears” (awali) and “high deeds” (ma'ali) chime.

translation: Ask the Arabs and the Turks what our hands did
in the land of Ubayd Allah's tomb.
2.sharh: He calls on Arabs and Turks alike to say what his people's hands did at that place. The question is a boast: he knows what they will answer.

translation: When we set out, our resolve did not weaken
before what we sought, and our efforts did not fail.
3.sharh: Once his people set out for revenge, nothing softened their resolve or wasted their effort; they got what they came for.

translation: O day of the battle of Zawra' in Iraq,
when we did to our enemies what they used to do to us.
4.sharh: He hails the day of the battle of al-Zawra', when his people paid their enemies back in kind and subdued them as they had once been subdued. The verb recalls the proverb “as you treat others, so you will be treated”.

translation: On lean horses we kept tethered and marked
only to raid those who were raiding us,
5.sharh: His people rode to battle on lean, trained war horses, kept ready only for those who attacked them: they defend, they do not start wars.

translation: and young men who, when we speak, bend their ears
to our words, and when we call them, answer.
6.sharh: With them rode young men who listened when their leaders spoke and answered when they were called to fight.

translation: A people who, when challenged, are pharaohs,
and when made judges, are scales.
7.sharh: Challenged, they are as overbearing as Pharaoh; asked to judge between others, they weigh as fairly as a balance. Ferocity is for the enemy, justice for those who come to them.

translation: They wear reason as their cloak, but when
the fire of war grows hot, you would think them mad.
8.sharh: In peace they are calm and sensible; once battle blazes they fight with such abandon, so careless of death, that they seem to have lost their minds.

translation: When they claim a thing, the world comes to confirm it;
when they pray, the days say “Amen”.
9.sharh: Whatever they claim, events bear out; whatever they pray for, time grants, as if the days themselves said Amen. “Claim” (idda'aw) and “pray” (da'aw) come from one root.

translation: The starlings, once their cause rose up,
imagined they had turned into falcons.
10.sharh: He turns to the enemy: weak little birds that, once they gained some strength, took themselves for birds of prey, upstarts who thought a moment's power made them his people's equals.

translation: They took the grey hawks' patience for fear,
not knowing it was only disdain.
11.sharh: The enemy mistook his people's restraint for cowardice; in truth the hawks did not think the starlings worth the chase.

translation: Pawns that the rooks' hands had captured:
had we left them alone, they would have hunted queens.
12.sharh: The enemies are chess pawns, the weakest pieces, taken by the rooks; left alone they would have overreached and brought down pieces far above them, so his people cut them down in time.

translation: Our swords kept them humble for ages, but once
they had power, they showed us their hatred.
13.sharh: Long held down by his people's swords, the enemy turned on them as soon as they had a share of power, and old grudges came into the open.

translation: Our wealth was not enough for them; they plundered our lives,
as if they were safe from our coming to collect.
14.sharh: Not content with robbing his people, the enemy took their lives, as though no one would ever come to collect. Blood is a debt here, and revenge its repayment.

translation: They emptied the mosques of our elders and went too far,
until we charged and emptied the offices of state.
15.sharh: The enemy killed his people's elders in their mosques, an allusion to his uncle, murdered in his own; his people charged and cleared the enemy out of the offices of government. The repeated verb makes the revenge exact.

translation: Then we turned back, our swords still swaying
with pride, and the spears quivering supple.
16.sharh: They rode home with their weapons strutting like victors: the swords sway, proud of what they have done, and the spears bend and quiver.

translation: On our clothes the blood has left clots
whose scent spares us the need of musk.
17.sharh: The dried blood of their enemies on their clothes smells sweeter to them than any perfume: the blood of vengeance is their musk.

translation: What a call it was, travelling across the earth,
now a lesson on the lips of time.
18.sharh: The story of their call to vengeance has spread through the world and become something the ages repeat, like a lesson recited until it is known by heart.

translation: We are a people whose nobility of character forbids us
to harm first anyone who does not harm us.
19.sharh: Their sense of honour forbids them to strike first. What they did was retaliation, not aggression, the claim already made in line 5.

translation: White are our favours, black our battles,
green our pastures, red our blades.
20.sharh: Four colours for four boasts: their kindness is spotless, their battles are dark days for the enemy, their lands are green with plenty, their swords red with blood.

translation: No weakness shows in us short of winning what we wish,
even if we saw death waiting in our hopes.
21.sharh: They never flag before they reach their goal, even when the way to it runs through death. In Arabic “deaths” (manaya) and “hopes” (amani) are almost the same letters.

translation: Whenever we lacked firmans to attack by,
we made our swords our firmans.
22.sharh: If they had no royal decree to fight by, their swords became the decree, giving the orders and carrying them out. The last word repeats the first half's “firmans”.

translation: When we run a heat in the race for glory,
if we do not come first, we come close behind.
23.sharh: Glory is a horse race, and in every heat they finish first, or right behind the first; they are never further back than that.

translation: Our resolve wards off even sealed fate
from us, and we could outargue time's blows if we chose.
24.sharh: The boast goes as far as it can: their will pushes back what fate has decreed, and they could beat the blows of time in open dispute, if they cared to.

translation: We wade into troubles with our own hands and push them back,
and when they strike us, we push them off with our own hands.
25.sharh: They take on hardship of their own accord and beat it off, and when it falls on them unasked they deal with it themselves. Ending both halves on “hands” stresses that they rely on no one else.

translation: A sovereign power: when the enemy's arrows are notched against us,
its resolve shoots whoever would shoot at us,
26.sharh: He praises a sovereign power that protects his people: when an enemy fits his arrows to the string against them, its resolve shoots him.

translation: resolve like the shooting stars, and as piercing,
with which it never stops burning devils.
27.sharh: That resolve strikes their enemies as shooting stars strike devils; in the Quran, devils who try to eavesdrop on heaven are driven off by a piercing flame (37:10).

translation: It gave, and its giving was no slip
on its part, nor was its reward spoiled by reproach.
28.sharh: Its gifts are deliberate, never an accident, and it never reminds anyone of what it gave. The second half echoes the Quran's promise of “a reward unfailing” (95:6).

translation: Many an enemy of ours, for all his might,
has shown us submission, to trick us and lull us,
29.sharh: Some enemies, strong as they are, put on a show of submission only to trick his people into lowering their guard.

translation: like the viper that is smooth to the touch
until it finds a firm hold on a limb.
30.sharh: Such an enemy is a snake, soft under the hand until it has a hold and can bite: his meekness is a cover for treachery.

translation: He wraps treachery for us inside the advice he gives,
mixes poison into honey, and gives us to drink.
31.sharh: He passes them betrayal folded inside advice, as poison is given in honey: sweet on the surface, deadly underneath.

translation: We lower our eyes and look past his foul deeds,
and it was not weakness that made us look away.
32.sharh: They bore with him out of forbearance, not because they could do nothing. In the diwan one more line follows, which the reciter leaves out: they let him be, trusting the emir to repay him.
